fields.Radiologic: CT or catheter angiography shows high-grade stenosis or occlusion of at least two of the celiac, superior mesenteric, and inferior mesenteric arteries. Enlarged collaterals, including the arc of Riolan and the marginal artery, bridge the occlusions.
fields.Pathology: Atherosclerotic narrowing at the origins of the mesenteric arteries. The bowel is intact between attacks.
fields.Inclusion: Chronic arterial insufficiency of the gut. Acute mesenteric ischemia is already listed and infarcts the bowel. Median arcuate ligament syndrome is a separate topic.

fields.Synonyms: Portal vein thrombosis, pylephlebitis, septic thrombophlebitis of the portal vein, acute portomesenteric venous thrombosis
fields.Clinical: Abdominal pain. Pylephlebitis adds fever and a source such as appendicitis or diverticulitis. Chronic thrombosis presents with variceal bleeding when the liver is not cirrhotic.
fields.Radiologic: CT or Doppler ultrasound shows a filling defect in the portal vein. Pylephlebitis adds liver abscesses and, sometimes, gas in the portal vein. Cavernous transformation is the chronic form.
fields.Pathology: Thrombus in the portal vein. In pylephlebitis the thrombus contains neutrophils and bacteria.
fields.Inclusion: Thrombosis of the portal vein. Budd-Chiari syndrome is already listed and blocks the hepatic veins. Cirrhotic portal hypertension is already listed.

fields.Synonyms: Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, hepatic veno-occlusive disease, SOS, VOD
fields.Clinical: Tender hepatomegaly, fluid weight gain, and jaundice in the weeks after hematopoietic-cell transplantation or after chemotherapy that injures sinusoids.
fields.Radiologic: Doppler ultrasound shows ascites, hepatomegaly, and slowed or reversed portal flow. The hepatic veins stay open. Contrast CT shows patchy liver enhancement.
fields.Pathology: Sinusoidal endothelial injury, sinusoidal congestion, and occlusion of central venules by fibrosis. The large hepatic veins are open.
fields.Inclusion: Sinusoidal and central-venule injury after transplantation or chemotherapy. Budd-Chiari syndrome is already listed and thromboses the hepatic veins. Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease is a different disease.

name: Congestive Hepatopathy and Fontan-Associated Liver Disease

fields.Synonyms: Nutmeg liver, cardiac cirrhosis, passive hepatic congestion, Fontan-associated liver disease, FALD
fields.Clinical: A person with right-heart failure or a Fontan circulation who develops hepatomegaly, ascites, or liver nodules years later.
fields.Radiologic: Delayed CT or MRI shows reticular enhancement of the liver periphery. The hepatic veins and the inferior vena cava are dilated. Fontan livers also form hypervascular nodules.
fields.Pathology: The cut surface is the nutmeg liver, with dark congested centers and pale periportal zones. Fibrosis bridges central veins. Cirrhosis comes late.
fields.Inclusion: Hepatic venous congestion. Budd-Chiari syndrome is already listed and is thrombotic outflow block. Decompensated cirrhosis from other causes is already listed.

fields.Synonyms: Paraduodenal pancreatitis, cystic dystrophy of the duodenum, pancreaticoduodenal groove pancreatitis
fields.Clinical: A middle-aged man who drinks alcohol, with pain, vomiting, and weight loss from duodenal narrowing.
fields.Radiologic: CT or MRI shows sheet-like tissue in the groove between the pancreatic head and the duodenum. The duodenal wall is thick and contains cysts. The bile duct may be smoothly narrowed.
fields.Pathology: Scarring and cysts in the duodenal wall and the pancreatic groove. Ectopic pancreatic tissue is often present. The rest of the pancreas may show ordinary chronic pancreatitis.
fields.Inclusion: A scar in the pancreaticoduodenal groove. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is already listed and is an infiltrative mass. Type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis is already inside IgG4-related disease.

fields.Synonyms: Malignant peritoneal mesothelioma, diffuse malignant peritoneal mesothelioma
fields.Clinical: Abdominal pain, distension from ascites, and weight loss. Asbestos exposure is common and is not required.
fields.Radiologic: CT shows ascites, omental and peritoneal masses, and mesenteric thickening. There is no ovarian or gastrointestinal primary. Calcified pleural plaques may be present.
fields.Pathology: Epithelioid, sarcomatoid, or biphasic mesothelioma. Calretinin, WT1, and cytokeratin 5/6 support the diagnosis. Loss of BAP1 supports it further.
fields.Inclusion: A primary peritoneal malignancy. Malignant pleural mesothelioma is already in Pulmonology. Pseudomyxoma peritonei is already listed and is mucinous.

fields.Synonyms: Cryptosporidium infection, Cryptosporidium parvum enteritis, Cryptosporidium hominis enteritis
fields.Clinical: Watery diarrhea. In an immunocompetent person it lasts days to weeks. In AIDS or after transplantation it is prolonged and severe.
fields.Radiologic: Imaging is nonspecific. The teaching images are the stool stain and the duodenal biopsy.
fields.Pathology: Acid-fast oocysts in the stool. On biopsy, round organisms sit on the surface of the small-bowel epithelium, and the villi are blunted.
fields.Inclusion: An acid-fast protozoan of the small-bowel surface. Giardiasis is a separate topic and shows pear-shaped trophozoites that are not acid-fast.

fields.Synonyms: Coin in the esophagus, ingested coin, esophageal foreign body from a coin
fields.Clinical: A toddler who drools, refuses food, or coughs after being seen with a coin. Many children have no symptoms.
fields.Radiologic: A frontal radiograph shows the coin as a round disc in the esophagus. On the lateral view the coin is seen on edge. A button battery instead shows a double ring or halo.
fields.Pathology: A retained coin presses on the mucosa. There is no caustic burn. Histology is not used to make the diagnosis.
fields.Inclusion: The common blunt esophageal foreign body. Button-battery ingestion is already listed and has the double-ring sign and a caustic burn.

fields.Synonyms: Ingested magnets, neodymium magnet ingestion, magnet foreign body of the bowel
fields.Clinical: A child who has swallowed more than one magnet. Pain and vomiting mean the magnets have pinched bowel between them.
fields.Radiologic: A radiograph shows two or more radiopaque disks stuck together, or a gap where bowel wall lies between them. Serial films show that the pair does not move.
fields.Pathology: Pressure necrosis and a fistula or perforation where the magnets have attracted across two loops.
fields.Inclusion: A small-bowel injury from magnets. Button-battery ingestion and esophageal coin ingestion are separate topics.

fields.Synonyms: Hepatic EHE, epithelioid hemangioendothelioma of the liver
fields.Clinical: A young adult with right-upper-quadrant pain or an incidental multifocal liver tumor. The course is often slow.
fields.Radiologic: CT or MRI shows multiple target lesions that coalesce under the capsule. The capsule retracts over the lesions. Enhancement is peripheral.
fields.Pathology: Epithelioid and dendritic cells in a myxoid or fibrous stroma, with intracytoplasmic vacuoles that mimic glands. The cells express vascular markers.
fields.Inclusion: A multifocal vascular liver tumor with capsular retraction. Hepatic hemangioma is a separate topic and fills in from the periphery. Cholangiocarcinoma is already listed.

fields.Synonyms: Autosomal dominant polycystic liver disease, PCLD, isolated polycystic liver
fields.Clinical: Abdominal distension and early satiety from a liver replaced by cysts. Kidney function is normal. Some patients need fenestration or transplantation.
fields.Radiologic: CT or MRI shows innumerable cysts throughout the liver. The kidneys do not contain the cysts of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.
fields.Pathology: The cysts are lined by biliary epithelium and do not communicate with the ducts.
fields.Inclusion: A polycystic liver without polycystic kidneys. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is already in Nephrology and often includes liver cysts as part of that disease.

fields.Synonyms: Xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis, fibroxanthogranulomatous cholecystitis
fields.Clinical: A long bout of right-upper-quadrant pain, fever, and a mass that feels like gallbladder carcinoma.
fields.Radiologic: CT shows marked gallbladder-wall thickening, intramural hypoattenuating nodules, and stones. The nodules may extend into the liver.
fields.Pathology: Foamy macrophages, giant cells, and bile pigment in the wall. Malignant epithelium is absent.
fields.Inclusion: A carcinoma mimic of the gallbladder. Gallbladder carcinoma is already listed. Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis is a different disease in the kidney.

name: Secondary Sclerosing Cholangitis of Critical Illness

fields.Synonyms: Sclerosing cholangitis in critically ill patients, SSC-CIP, ischemic cholangiopathy, secondary sclerosing cholangitis
fields.Clinical: Cholestasis that appears during a long intensive-care stay, often after shock, burns, or severe trauma. Jaundice rises as the patient otherwise recovers.
fields.Radiologic: Cholangiography shows casts filling the intrahepatic ducts, multifocal strictures, and ducts that no longer fill. The extrahepatic duct is relatively spared at first.
fields.Pathology: Biliary casts and injury of the biliary epithelium. The onionskin periductal fibrosis of primary sclerosing cholangitis is absent early.
fields.Inclusion: Ischemic injury of the bile ducts in critical illness. Primary sclerosing cholangitis and AIDS cholangiopathy are already listed.

fields.Synonyms: Hepatobiliary mucinous cystic neoplasm, biliary cystadenoma, mucinous cystic neoplasm of the liver
fields.Clinical: A middle-aged woman with a large liver cyst, pain, or a palpable mass.
fields.Radiologic: CT or MRI shows a multiloculated cyst in the liver, with septa and sometimes mural nodules. It does not connect to the bile ducts.
fields.Pathology: Mucinous epithelium and ovarian-type stroma, the same pair that defines pancreatic mucinous cystic neoplasm.
fields.Inclusion: A mucinous cyst of the liver. Isolated polycystic liver disease is a separate topic. Cystic echinococcosis is already in Infectious Diseases.

fields.Synonyms: Dubin-Johnson syndrome, chronic idiopathic jaundice, ABCC2 deficiency
fields.Clinical: Mild conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and intermittent jaundice that starts in adolescence. Pruritus and liver failure are absent.
fields.Radiologic: The liver is not scarred on imaging. Cholescintigraphy shows delayed or absent excretion into the bile.
fields.Pathology: The liver is grossly black or dark green. Coarse brown pigment sits in centrilobular hepatocytes.
fields.Inclusion: Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with a black liver. The gross pigment is how the syndrome is recognized.

name: Undifferentiated Embryonal Sarcoma of the Liver

fields.Synonyms: Undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma, embryonal sarcoma of the liver, malignant mesenchymoma of the liver
fields.Clinical: A school-age child with a rapidly enlarging liver mass, pain, and fever.
fields.Radiologic: CT shows a large cystic-appearing mass with solid nodules. Ultrasound shows that the lesion is predominantly solid. The discrepancy between the two studies is characteristic.
fields.Pathology: Spindle and stellate cells in a myxoid stroma, with PAS-positive diastase-resistant globules. Epithelial differentiation is absent.
fields.Inclusion: A cystic-looking pediatric liver sarcoma. Hepatoblastoma is already in Pediatrics. Mesenchymal hamartoma is a separate benign cystic mass of infants.

fields.Synonyms: Mesenchymal hamartoma, hepatic mesenchymal hamartoma
fields.Clinical: An infant with a large, painless abdominal mass. Fluid can make the mass grow quickly.
fields.Radiologic: Ultrasound and CT show a multicystic liver mass with thin septa. Solid stromal areas are present. Calcification is uncommon.
fields.Pathology: Disorganized bile ducts, vessels, and loose mesenchyme around cysts. The cysts contain serous or gelatinous fluid.
fields.Inclusion: A benign cystic liver mass of infants. Undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma is the malignant mass of older children. Cystic echinococcosis is already listed.

fields.Synonyms: Spigelian hernia, lateral ventral hernia, obturator hernia, hernia through the obturator canal
fields.Clinical: A Spigelian hernia is a tender mass along the semilunar line, often below the umbilicus. An obturator hernia presents in a thin older woman with obstruction and pain down the medial thigh, the Howship-Romberg sign.
fields.Radiologic: CT shows bowel leaving through a defect at the semilunar line, or bowel between the pectineus and obturator externus muscles. The obturator hernia compresses the obturator nerve.
fields.Pathology: A peritoneal sac through the Spigelian fascia or the obturator canal. Strangulated bowel is ischemic.
fields.Inclusion: Two uncommon hernias with disease-specific CT sites. Inguinal, femoral, and ventral hernias are already listed.

fields.Synonyms: Esophageal intramural pseudodiverticulosis, intramural esophageal diverticulosis
fields.Clinical: Intermittent dysphagia in an older adult. A stricture is often present. Candida may be found and does not explain the outpouchings.
fields.Radiologic: A barium esophagram shows many tiny flask-shaped outpouchings in the esophageal wall. A stricture, often in the upper or mid-esophagus, may accompany them.
fields.Pathology: Dilated excretory ducts of the submucosal esophageal glands. The flasks are not true diverticula through the muscle.
fields.Inclusion: A barium pattern of intramural flasks. Esophageal candidiasis is already listed and shows mucosal plaques. Zenker diverticulum is already listed and is a pharyngeal pouch.

fields.Synonyms: Gastric wall emphysema from infection, infectious gastritis with intramural gas
fields.Clinical: A toxic patient with severe abdominal pain and vomiting. The vomit may contain blood or sloughed mucosa. Diabetes and corrosive ingestion are settings.
fields.Radiologic: CT shows gas within a thick stomach wall. Portal venous gas may be present. The patient is ill, which separates this from benign gastric emphysema.
fields.Pathology: Necrosis of the stomach wall with gas-forming bacteria. The mucosa sloughs.
fields.Inclusion: Infectious gas in the stomach wall. Emphysematous cholecystitis is a separate topic and involves the gallbladder.

fields.Synonyms: Strawberry gallbladder, cholesterolosis, cholesterol polyposis of the gallbladder
fields.Clinical: Usually found in a gallbladder removed for stones. There are no specific symptoms.
fields.Radiologic: Ultrasound may show cholesterol polyps as small nonshadowing spots fixed to the wall. The gross specimen is the teaching image.
fields.Pathology: The mucosa is red with yellow flecks of lipid, the strawberry gallbladder. Foamy macrophages fill the lamina propria.
fields.Inclusion: A gross pathology diagnosis of the gallbladder mucosa. Gallstones and gallbladder carcinoma are already listed.

fields.Synonyms: Enteric duplication cyst, ileal duplication, gastrointestinal duplication
fields.Clinical: A child with a mass, obstruction, or bleeding. Gastric mucosa inside the cyst can ulcerate the adjacent bowel.
fields.Radiologic: Ultrasound shows a cyst with the gut signature: an inner hyperechoic mucosa and an outer hypoechoic muscle layer. The cyst wall may peristalse.
fields.Pathology: A cyst that shares a wall or a blood supply with the bowel. The lining is gastrointestinal epithelium, and a smooth-muscle layer is present.
fields.Inclusion: A congenital cyst with the gut-signature wall. Meckel diverticulum is already listed and is an outpouching of the ileum, not a closed cyst.

fields.Synonyms: Ancylostoma duodenale infection, Necator americanus infection, intestinal hookworm
fields.Clinical: Iron-deficiency anemia, fatigue, and abdominal discomfort after exposure to contaminated soil. A heavy infection causes edema from protein loss.
fields.Radiologic: Endoscopy shows small worms attached to the duodenal or jejunal mucosa, with blood at the attachment sites.
fields.Pathology: The stool contains thin-shelled hookworm eggs. The adult worm attaches by a buccal capsule.
fields.Inclusion: A blood-feeding worm seen on endoscopy. Ascariasis and strongyloidiasis are already in Infectious Diseases and look different. Cutaneous larva migrans is the skin track of animal hookworm and is a different disease.

fields.Synonyms: Yersinia ileitis, Yersinia enterocolitis, Yersinia mesenteric adenitis
fields.Clinical: Hemorrhagic bullae, necrosis, and scars exactly at mosquito-bite sites
fields.Radiologic: Ultrasound or CT shows thickening of the terminal ileum and enlarged mesenteric nodes. The appendix may be normal.
fields.Pathology: Lymphoid hyperplasia and ulceration of the terminal ileum. Stool culture or PCR identifies Yersinia enterocolitica. The chronic fissuring ulcers of Crohn disease are absent.
fields.Inclusion: An infectious terminal ileitis. Crohn disease and acute appendicitis are already listed. Plague is Yersinia pestis and is a different disease.

name: Fibrous pseudotumor of the tunica vaginalis
Webs, bands, mosaic perfusion, and a mismatched ventilation-perfusion scan. Acute pulmonary embolism is already listed.

fields.Synonyms: CTEPH, chronic thromboembolic disease
fields.Clinical: Dyspnea and signs of right-heart failure months or years after pulmonary emboli. Some patients have no known acute embolus. A loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound and edema are late findings.
fields.Radiologic: The ventilation-perfusion scan shows mismatched segmental defects. CT and pulmonary angiography show webs, bands, pouch defects, and abrupt cutoffs. The right ventricle is hypertrophied. The surgical specimen is a cast of organized thrombus.
fields.Pathology: Organized thrombus is incorporated into the pulmonary artery wall, with recanalized channels and fibrous webs. At thromboendarterectomy the material peels away as a recognizable cast.
fields.Inclusion: A treatable pulmonary hypertension with webs and a surgical cast. Acute pulmonary embolism is already in Pulmonology and is the fresh clot, not the organized web.
